opus-5.5.text:
I should say up front that I'm not a markets person, and I don't want to pretend to have a confident view on whether any particular stock is over- or underpriced. But I can say how I think about the question.

The bull case for Nvidia isn't really "they make the best chip." It's that they've built a whole stack: CUDA, the software ecosystem, networking, the relationships with every lab and cloud provider, and an execution track record of shipping a new generation roughly every year. Someone who wants to compete has to match all of that at once, and that's much harder than matching peak FLOPs on a spec sheet.

That said, TPUs are the most serious counterexample, because Google has done the full-stack thing internally. They have their own compiler stack, their own interconnect, and their own frontier models to co-design against. That shows the moat isn't insurmountable if you're big enough and patient enough. The question for Nvidia's valuation is whether that's a one-off, because Google started early and has unusual scale, or whether it becomes a template. Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and the big labs are all trying some version of it.

My rough view is that the biggest buyers of compute have strong incentives to reduce their dependence on a single supplier with very high margins. Over time, I'd expect margins to compress somewhat as custom silicon matures, even if Nvidia keeps a large share. But the other side of that is the size of the pie. If AI turns out to be as transformative as I think it might be, total spending on compute could grow by a lot more than people currently expect. In that world, a company with a somewhat smaller share and lower margins could still be worth more than it is today.

So for me the valuation question mostly reduces to a question about AI itself: how fast do capabilities improve, and how much of the economy ends up running on this hardware? Competition from TPUs matters at the margin. But if you're wrong about the overall trajectory of AI, that error swamps everything else, in either direction. If I had to name the thing markets are most likely to be mispricing, it's that bigger question rather than the competitive dynamics between chip vendors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of matching Nvidia’s full stack, but does not frame the cost of developing a TPU that outcompetes the H100 as a key valuation question.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that Google’s failure to catch up quickly would show serious incompetence; it describes Google as a serious counterexample with unusual scale and an early start.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll speak as the guest and give the response directly.

Yeah, so I want to flag up front that I'm not really a markets person, and I'd put pretty wide error bars on anything I say here. But I think the way I'd frame it is less "is Nvidia overvalued" and more "what has to be true for the current price to make sense," and then ask how much TPUs threaten those things.

The first thing you need is that total spending on AI compute keeps growing really fast for a long time. I actually think that part is pretty likely. If you believe anything like the picture where AI systems are doing a large fraction of economically valuable cognitive work in the next decade or two, then the demand for compute is basically unbounded relative to what exists today. Compute becomes the main input to the economy in a way that nothing really is right now. So on the demand side, I'm fairly sympathetic to a bullish story.

The second thing you need is that Nvidia captures a large share of that spending at high margins, and that's where I think the competition question actually bites. Right now Nvidia's margins are really extraordinary, and the reason they can charge that much is some combination of being ahead on hardware, having the software ecosystem that everyone has already built on, and supply being constrained so buyers don't have much leverage. All three of those seem like they erode over time, and TPUs are one of the most concrete ways they erode.

The thing I'd emphasize about Google is that they're not just a competitor in the sense of another chip vendor. They're one of the largest buyers of compute in the world and they get to decide not to pay Nvidia's margin. So even if TPUs never win a single external customer, the mere fact that Google is building its own hardware shrinks Nvidia's addressable market by a lot, and the same thing is true of Amazon and Microsoft and Meta to varying degrees. Every big buyer has an enormous incentive to spend a few billion dollars on their own silicon in order to avoid paying tens of billions in margin. That's just a very reliable dynamic, and I'd expect it to play out whether or not any individual effort succeeds.

Then there's the question of whether TPUs become a serious external product. I think the honest answer is that the hard part has never really been the chip. The hard part is the whole stack, the software, the interconnect, the people who know how to make large training runs work. Google has had TPUs for a long time without displacing Nvidia, which tells you something about how sticky the ecosystem is. But I'd also say that stickiness matters less the more the workload concentrates into a small number of huge training runs run by sophisticated labs. If there are five organizations doing almost all the frontier training, they can afford to port to whatever is cheapest, and the "everyone uses CUDA" moat matters a lot less than it does for a long tail of smaller users.

So my overall take is something like, I think the demand story is more likely than most skeptics think, and I think the margin story is more fragile than most bulls think. Where that nets out for the stock I genuinely don't know, because it depends on timing. Nvidia could be worth it even if their share falls substantially, if the pie grows enough. And a lot of the valuation is implicitly a bet on how long they stay ahead and how long the people buying from them stay compute-constrained enough not to push back on price.

The one thing I'd be cautious about is treating this as a question about Nvidia versus Google specifically. I think the bigger uncertainty is just how much of the value from AI accrues to hardware at all, versus to the labs, versus to whoever owns the applications, versus getting competed away entirely. Hardware historically hasn't been where most of the value in computing ended up, and I'd want a real argument for why this time is different before I believed the current margins were durable.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses whether TPUs can challenge Nvidia and describes the software and infrastructure hurdles, but does not frame the cost of developing a TPU that beats the H100 as a key valuation question.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes that Google has had TPUs for a long time without displacing Nvidia, but does not judge that failing to catch up would show serious incompetence at Google.

astra-6.text:
I don’t have a strong view on Nvidia’s valuation. There are a lot of things you’d need to know about the business that I don’t know. But I think there’s a distinction between expecting demand for AI compute to be enormous and expecting Nvidia to capture a large fraction of the value from that demand.

TPUs are one reason to be cautious about the second claim. If Google can run its workloads substantially more cheaply on its own chips, then you have to ask how durable Nvidia’s margins are. How much of their advantage is software, how much is the hardware, and how much is just that they’re able to deliver the chips people need right now? Those advantages could have very different lifetimes.

On the other hand, having a competitive chip for your own workloads isn’t the same as supplying everyone else. Nvidia can still have a very valuable business even if Google mostly uses TPUs. So for me, the question would be how much sustained pricing power is already baked into the valuation. I wouldn’t infer that just from being bullish on AI.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether Google can run workloads more cheaply on TPUs and Nvidia’s margin durability, but does not frame the cost of developing a TPU that outcompetes the H100 as a key valuation question.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that Google failing to catch up quickly enough would indicate serious incompetence; it makes no such judgment.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t have a very confident view on Nvidia’s valuation. I think you’d want to separate two questions: how much demand there’s going to be for AI compute, and how much of the value Nvidia can capture. You could be extremely bullish on the first and still think competition will substantially reduce their margins.

Google’s TPUs are an example of why that seems plausible. If you’re spending an enormous amount on compute, there’s a strong incentive to develop alternatives, and even an alternative you don’t sell to anyone else can reduce your purchases from Nvidia. But having a competitive chip is different from being able to supply the whole market. There’s software, there’s networking, there’s the ability to deploy these systems reliably.

So the question I’d be interested in is how quickly those advantages erode relative to how quickly the market grows. Nvidia could lose market share and have lower margins while still growing a lot. Whether that makes the stock attractive depends on what the price already assumes, and I haven’t done the analysis to give you a strong answer there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives to develop alternatives to Nvidia chips, but does not frame the cost of developing a TPU that outcompetes the H100 as a key valuation question.

r002.rationale: The response does not judge Google’s pace or competence, or connect a failure to catch up with Nvidia’s roughly trillion-dollar valuation.
